locations.name: Kingaroy
locations.depot: our own Lockyer Valley yard, run north through the Brisbane Valley
locations.leadTime: Usually 3–5 business days; we group South Burnett runs where we can
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; side loader or crane truck for 40ft where the approach is wide enough
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Kingaroy and the South Burnett. Red soil, long farm driveways and cold winters allowed for. Ring for a price.
locations.line: Kingaroy sits far enough off the main freight routes that a container is worth ordering once and ordering properly. The run north through the Brisbane Valley and up over the Blackbutt Range is most of a day for a truck, so we would rather ask three questions about your gate now than turn a driver around at it later.
locations.uses: harvest gear that only earns its keep for six weeks a year, seed, fertiliser and bagged product kept off the ground and away from vermin, hay and silage covers, fencing wire, posts and strainers in one lockable place, machinery parts and spare tynes on properties where the shed filled up a decade ago, tools and materials for owner-builders on the rural-residential blocks around town, and dry storage for the small growers and vineyards through the district
access: The soil is the first thing anybody notices about the South Burnett and it is the first thing that decides a delivery. The deep red volcanic ground through Kingaroy, Kumbia and Wooroolin is friable and drains far better than the black soil country further west, which is genuinely good news — it does not turn into the grey glue that can shut a district down for a week. What it does instead is go slick on the surface within twenty minutes of rain while the metre underneath stays firm, so a loaded truck loses traction on a gentle grade long before the ground has any right to be a problem. Give it a day of sun and it is fine again. Force it on the morning after a storm and you have a pair of ruts across the paddock and a driver ringing your neighbour about a tractor. Distance from the gate is the second factor. Driveways run a long way out here, usually unsealed, usually crowned, and often with table drains either side that a rear wheel can drop into and not climb back out of. At the far end the truck needs somewhere it can line up straight and unload, because a tilt-tray does not place a container sideways and should not be reversing half a kilometre back to the road in fading light. Grids get asked about on every rural booking, because a lot of them out here were built by somebody's grandfather from whatever rail was going at the time and nobody now has the faintest idea what they carry. Then there are the ordinary things that stop a truck anywhere: gates that measure narrower than they look, a powerline strung to the pump shed at exactly the height a lifted bed wants, and old ironbarks with limbs hanging over the drive at four metres. A photo from the road looking in, and one of the spot itself, settles nearly all of it before anybody books a truck.

sections.h: Up the Blackbutt Range
p: The run to Kingaroy from our yard goes out through Fernvale and Esk, up the Brisbane Valley, and then climbs the Blackbutt Range on the D'Aguilar. That climb is the part that shapes everything else. It is steep, tightly cornered and timbered close to the road, and a loaded truck crawls it. There is no way to make it shorter and no point pretending otherwise, so what we do instead is plan around it: South Burnett deliveries get grouped where the dates allow, and we would rather put two containers on one trip than send a truck up that range twice in a fortnight.

For you that means two practical things. Give us a bit of notice where you can — a few days of flexibility usually buys a better spot in the run, and if you are ordering more than one unit, or you and a neighbour both need something, say so and we will look at doing it in one movement. And if you have a hard date, a shed being demolished, a harvest starting, a settlement, tell us at the enquiry rather than after we have quoted. Building the run around a fixed date is easy. Rebuilding it afterwards is not.

sections.h: Frosty mornings and what happens inside the box
p: Kingaroy gets real winters. Clear nights, heavy frost on the flats, and a swing of twenty degrees or more between dawn and mid-afternoon. A shipping container is uninsulated steel with a very large roof area, and it follows that swing closely. On a cold clear night the roof panel drops below the dew point of the air trapped inside, moisture condenses on the underside of it, and by morning it is running down the corrugations and dripping onto whatever is directly beneath. People notice the drips and assume the roof is leaking. Nine times in ten it is not — the water started on the inside.

It is manageable and it costs almost nothing to manage. Keep contents up off the floor on pallets or a couple of bearers so air can move underneath. Do not put anything in damp — a wet tarp or green timber shut in a steel box will keep the humidity high for months on its own. Fit extra vents if the unit is going to hold anything moisture-sensitive, and leave the doors open for a couple of hours on a dry, breezy day now and then to clear it out. On a long-term store holding tools, seed or paper records, a layer of insulation under the roof is worth the money and stops the problem at the source rather than mopping up after it.

sections.h: Peanut country, and gear that only works six weeks a year
p: A lot of what a South Burnett container ends up holding is seasonal — equipment that is flat out for a short window and then has to sit somewhere for ten months without seizing, rusting or being pulled apart for parts by whoever needs a bolt. That is what a container is genuinely good at. It arrives finished, it locks, it keeps birds and vermin out, and every cargo-worthy unit is checked wind and watertight before it leaves our yard, so what goes in dry stays dry. It also does not require a slab, an approval process or six months of waiting, which matters when the alternative is a shed you have been meaning to build since 2019. Set it on hardwood sleepers or concrete pads at the four corner castings, door end on the high side of any fall, and it will still be sitting square and opening cleanly long after the machinery inside it has been replaced twice.

faqs.q: Can you deliver onto red soil after a wet week?
faqs.a: Usually, once it has had a day or so of sun on it. South Burnett red soil drains well and firms up quickly, but the top surface goes slippery fast, and a loaded truck loses grip on a gentle rise well before the ground itself is soft. We would rather ring you and move a delivery by a couple of days than leave ruts across your paddock or tie a truck up waiting on a tractor. If you have a hardstand or a firm spot near the road, tell us — we can often set the container down there and let you shift it in at your own pace.

faqs.q: How far out into the South Burnett will you come?
faqs.a: Right across it. Nanango, Wondai, Murgon, Kumbia, Blackbutt, Yarraman, Proston and Goomeri are all normal drops for us, and so are the properties well off the bitumen between them. What changes with distance is not whether we will come but how the run gets scheduled, because the range climb makes a South Burnett trip a committed day rather than a quick shuttle. Give us the address and a rough idea of your timing and we will tell you where it fits.

faqs.q: Do containers get damp inside through a Kingaroy winter?
faqs.a: They can, and it is condensation rather than a leaking roof almost every time. Cold clear nights drop the steel below the dew point of the air inside, moisture forms on the underside of the roof and drips. Keep contents on pallets so air moves, do not store anything damp in there to begin with, add vents if the unit is holding moisture-sensitive gear, and open the doors on a dry breezy day occasionally. For a long-term store, insulating under the roof solves it properly.

faqs.q: Can I store seed or grain in a shipping container?
faqs.a: Bagged product, seed, fertiliser and the gear that goes with it, absolutely — it stays dry, it locks, and vermin and birds cannot get at it. What a container is not is a sealed silo. It is not built to be gas-tight and it should not be treated as a substitute for proper sealed storage where that is what the job requires. For bulk grain handling, use the equipment designed for it. For everything around the edges of that operation, a container does the job well and is available now rather than next season.

locations.name: Tweed Heads
locations.depot: the south-east Queensland depots, a short run down the motorway and across the border
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days; add a day where a crane and a street closure have to line up
locations.truck: Tilt-tray where there is a straight run in; crane truck for waterfront blocks, villages and over-fence lifts
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Tweed Heads, Banora Point and Kingscliff. Waterfront blocks, ridge driveways and cane flats each handled differently.
locations.line: Tweed Heads is a short haul on a good road and then it stops being simple. The blocks nearest the water have no side access at all, the ridge suburbs behind town are steep and tightly cornered, and the flats out toward the cane are soft ground with the water table sitting close underneath. None of that is unworkable. It is just worth naming before a truck leaves the depot.
locations.uses: boats, skis and fishing gear where the garage lost that argument years ago, site stores on the steady run of knockdown-rebuilds through Banora Point and Kingscliff, tools and stock for trades working both sides of the border in the one week, linen and equipment for holiday letting operators between changeovers, cane and small-crop gear on the flats around Chinderah and Cudgen, and lock-up storage for people moving into a village and discovering that forty years of things do not fit
access: Start with the border, because everyone asks and it is the least interesting part of the job. The truck comes down the motorway and crosses at Tweed. It is a state line on a map, not a checkpoint, and the only real consequence is that New South Wales road rules and heavy vehicle conditions apply from that point south. We do it constantly. It changes nothing about your delivery date. What does change your delivery is which of the three Tweeds you live in. The waterfront and canal blocks through Tweed Heads West, Tweed Heads South and the lower part of Banora Point are wide at the water and narrow at the street, with the house filling the block and a side gate you could not get a ride-on through. Those are crane jobs, not tilt-tray jobs, and the questions that decide them are all about what is overhead and how much street the outriggers can have. The ridge suburbs are the opposite problem. Terranora, Bilambil Heights and the streets climbing out of Banora are steep, cambered and tightly cornered, with driveways that pitch away hard at the kerb and carports built at a height nobody imagined a tilt bed under. Plenty of those blocks work. Some of them work only with a smaller unit than you had in mind. Then the flats. Out through Chinderah, Cudgen, Tumbulgum and up the valley the ground is cane country — alluvial soil over a shallow water table, firm under a dry crust and soft the moment you break through it, cut about with farm drains and reached by narrow roads with single-lane bridges on them. And the coastal strip at Fingal Head, Kingscliff and Casuarina is dune sand, which looks solid on a nature strip right up until a loaded rear axle proves otherwise.

sections.h: Crossing the border is the least of it
p: We get asked whether being in New South Wales complicates a delivery from Queensland, and the honest answer is no. The Tweed is one urban area with a state line drawn through the middle of it, thousands of vehicles cross it every hour, and a container truck is just one of them. The run down is short and the road is good. There is no border surcharge, no special arrangement and no delay built into it.

What is different south of the line is the paperwork behind the scenes rather than anything you experience — New South Wales road rules and heavy vehicle conditions apply, and any street occupancy for a crane goes through the council on this side rather than the Queensland one. We deal with that. The variable that actually decides your delivery is the last hundred metres onto your block, and that has nothing to do with which state you are in.

sections.h: Ridge driveways above the river
p: The streets climbing up to Terranora and Bilambil Heights were surveyed for the view rather than for a twelve-metre truck. They are narrow, steeply cambered, and they corner tightly enough that a rigid with a container overhanging the rear axle has to be driven for rather than simply driven. The driveways off them are the harder half: short, pitched hard down or hard up off the kerb, and frequently ending under a carport or against a garage door with no run past it. A tilt-tray needs the bed to come down without grounding out and the container needs somewhere straight to slide onto. On a lot of ridge blocks neither is available, and the answer is a crane truck standing on the street lifting over the fence, or a 20ft where a 40ft was the plan. Send us a photo taken from the middle of the road looking straight up the drive and another from where you want it standing, and we can usually call it in a phone call rather than on the morning.

sections.h: Villages, parks and the notice they need
p: The Tweed has a lot of over-50s villages, residential parks and holiday parks, and containers go into them regularly. The pattern is consistent: the internal roads are narrow with tight bends and speed humps, there are carport awnings and shade sails at heights a truck cannot argue with, and management needs to know a truck is coming rather than finding out when it arrives. Approval and a booked window are two separate things and both take a little lead time.

None of it is difficult and all of it is much easier a week out than on the day. Get the go-ahead from management first, ask them where a truck can legally stand and which way in they prefer, and check whether there is a height restriction anywhere on the route — a shade sail or a carport awning across an internal road will stop a delivery dead. It is also worth asking whether they want the truck outside peak movement times, because the internal roads in most of these parks are single-vehicle width and a truck sitting in one blocks everybody. The same applies to strata and gated estates on the coastal side. An hour of phone calls beforehand saves a truck standing at a boom gate with nobody available to open it.

faqs.q: Does delivering across the border from Queensland change anything?
faqs.a: Not in any way you will notice. The Tweed is one urban area with a state line through it and our trucks cross it constantly. New South Wales road rules apply once we are over, and if a crane needs street space the approval goes through the council on this side, but there is no border surcharge, no special arrangement and no delay built into the run. The thing that decides your delivery date is access at your end, not which state your letterbox is in.

faqs.q: Can a container get up a Terranora or Bilambil Heights driveway?
faqs.a: Often, though not always with a tilt-tray. Those streets are narrow and steeply cambered, and the driveways off them tend to pitch hard at the kerb and finish under a carport with no run past it, which is exactly what a tilt bed cannot work with. Where the drive will not take it, a crane truck lifting from the street over the fence usually will, and sometimes the sensible answer is a 20ft instead of a 40ft. A photo from the road looking up the drive tells us most of what we need.

faqs.q: Is the ground on the Tweed cane flats firm enough for a container?
faqs.a: It carries a container perfectly well once it is set up properly, but it will not carry it dumped straight onto the dirt. The flats are alluvial soil over a shallow water table, firm under a dry crust and soft as soon as that crust breaks, so each corner casting will punch in unevenly and the doors will stop lining up within a season. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, levelled both ways, fix it permanently and keep the floor clear of damp ground. Tell us the ground type at the quote and we will bring the timber.

faqs.q: Can you deliver into an over-50s village or a holiday park at Tweed Heads?
faqs.a: Yes, and we do it regularly. What makes it go smoothly is arranging it with management before you order rather than after. They will tell you where a truck can stand, which way in works, and whether there is a shade sail or awning on the route that a truck cannot get under. Internal roads in those parks are narrow with tight bends, so knowing the approach in advance matters more than usual. Get the approval and a preferred window first and we will build the booking around it.

locations.name: Ballina
locations.depot: the south-east Queensland depots, run south down the Pacific Highway
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days once the access questions are settled
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for tight coastal blocks; side loader for 40ft onto a farm with room
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Ballina, Lennox Head and Alstonville. Plateau farms, low river-flat ground and coastal blocks on their merits.
locations.line: Ballina is two pieces of country ten minutes apart. Up on the plateau there is deep red basalt soil, macadamias and avocados, and generally enough room to put a 40ft wherever you want it. Down on the flat at the river mouth there is old estuary ground, a water table you could nearly reach with a shovel, and blocks where the only way in is over the fence.
locations.uses: harvest and irrigation gear stored between seasons on the plateau orchards, nets, fittings and pump spares out of the weather, boats, boards and dive gear at Lennox Head and East Ballina, trade storage on the industrial land around Southern Cross Drive and Russellton, stock and equipment for the cafes, charters and tourism operators along the river, and household storage while a beach cottage gets knocked down and rebuilt into something twice the size
access: The Alstonville plateau is the easy half and it is easy for a specific reason: the soil. That deep red basalt is one of the best-behaved surfaces we deliver onto anywhere. It is free-draining, it holds structure when it is wet, and a loaded truck will get across it days after rain that would have shut a black-soil paddock. What the plateau gives you in ground it takes back in geometry. The roads up and off the escarpment are winding and hard against the bank in places, orchard rows are laid out for a tractor rather than a rigid truck, and there is irrigation main, low canopy and shade cloth strung at heights that a lifted bed will find first. Turning space between the trees is usually the constraint rather than the driveway itself. Down on the flat the problem reverses. West Ballina, Pimlico, Meerschaum Vale, Wardell and the ground behind the dunes are old estuarine deposits — soft, low, cut about with drains and levees, and holding water a couple of hundred millimetres below a surface that looks bone dry. Some of that country is acid sulfate soil, which is a reason to disturb it as little as possible rather than a reason to avoid it. A container sitting on pads on top is fine. A truck dragging a rut through it is not. Then the coastal blocks. East Ballina, Lennox Head, Skennars Head and Sharpes Beach are dune sand, and dry sand carries almost nothing — a nature strip that has taken cars for twenty years will still take a container truck's rear duals down to the axle. Add older beachside streets with the house hard against one boundary, a side gate built for a wheelbarrow and figs overhanging the frontage, and a good proportion of coastal Ballina jobs are crane lifts rather than drive-ins.

sections.h: Why the plateau is the easy half
p: If your address is Alstonville, Wollongbar, Tintenbar or the country between them, you are on some of the most cooperative delivery ground in the state. Red basalt drains hard and fast, it does not turn to grease the way alluvial or black soil does, and it means the wet does not shut you out for a week the way it can on the flats. That has a real practical benefit: plateau bookings hold up in weather that would move a river-flat delivery, so if you are choosing a date in a wet stretch, being up top is worth a lot.

The trade is space. Orchard access is laid out for machinery that is narrow and long, not for a truck that needs a straight run and somewhere to turn at the end of it. If the container is going in among the trees rather than up near the shed, walk the route first and look for the three things that actually stop us: the width between rows at the tightest point, the height of any irrigation main, shade cloth or low limb, and whether there is anywhere at the far end for the truck to line up straight. Where the rows will not take it, we can set the unit near the shed and you can shift it in with a tractor at your convenience.

sections.h: Old estuary ground on the flats
p: The low country around the river mouth is not soil in the way the plateau is soil. It is old estuary — silt and clay laid down when the sea was somewhere else, sitting a metre or so above a water table that never really goes away. In a dry September it forms a crust you would happily park on. Break through the crust and there is not much underneath, and a container corner casting concentrates a couple of tonne onto a footprint the size of a dinner plate, which is exactly the sort of load that finds a soft spot.

The fix is the same one we use on any soft ground and it is cheap: concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, bedded and checked level both ways and on the diagonals, so the load spreads and the floor sits clear of damp ground. On the flats we would generally go a bit further than usual and get the underside a hundred and fifty millimetres up so air moves under it, because a floor sitting hard against ground that is permanently moist is where a long-term store goes wrong — from below, not from the roof. Tell us what the ground is like when you enquire and we will bring the materials with us and do the levelling as part of the delivery.

sections.h: Cargo-worthy or as-is on a coastal block
p: This decision matters more within a couple of kilometres of the beach than it does inland, so it is worth being plain about. Every cargo-worthy unit is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard, and that is the grade to ask for if the container is living outdoors year-round with anything in it you would be annoyed to lose — tools, stock, household goods, anything with an electric motor in it. As-is units cost less and are entirely honest about what they are. They suit a site store for steel, formwork or gear that does not mind weather, and they have a real place. They are not sold as watertight and should not be bought as though they are, and on a salt-air block at Lennox or East Ballina that difference shows up sooner than it would out west. Tell us what is going inside and how long for, and we will point you at the one you need rather than the dearer one.

faqs.q: Can you deliver into an orchard on the Alstonville plateau?
faqs.a: Regularly, and the ground up there is rarely the limiting factor — red basalt carries a truck well even after rain. What stops us is geometry: row width at the tightest point, irrigation main or shade cloth strung low across the route, overhanging limbs, and whether there is room at the far end for the truck to line up straight before unloading. Walk the route and check those before you order. If the rows are too tight, we can set the container down near the shed and you can walk it in with a tractor.

faqs.q: How does low-lying ground at West Ballina hold a container?
faqs.a: Well enough, provided the container is set on something rather than dropped on the dirt. The flats are old estuary silt with a shallow water table, firm under a dry crust and soft underneath it, and each corner casting concentrates a serious point load into a small footprint. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, levelled in both directions, solve it permanently. On that ground we would also raise it enough to get air moving underneath, because a floor sitting against permanently damp soil is how a long-term store deteriorates from below.

faqs.q: Which grade suits a container sitting a few streets from the beach?
faqs.a: Cargo-worthy, for anything that has to stay dry. Every cargo-worthy unit is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard, which is what you want with salt air working on it year-round. As-is units are cheaper and genuinely useful where a dent or some surface rust is irrelevant, but they are not sold as watertight and that distinction shows up faster on the coast than it does inland. Tell us what is going in it and we will give you a straight answer rather than an upsell.

faqs.q: How much notice do you need for a Ballina delivery?
faqs.a: Two to four business days is the normal window once we know how the container is getting onto the block. The thing that adds time is not the haul, which is straightforward down the highway, but a crane booking on a tight coastal block or a stretch of wet weather that makes a low-lying site not worth risking. If you have a fixed date — a settlement, a build start, a removalist already booked — say so at the enquiry and we will schedule around it.

locations.name: Lismore
locations.depot: the south-east Queensland depots, run down the Pacific and west on the Bruxner
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days; river-flat drops move with the weather rather than against it
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck where the block is tight or the container is going up onto a stand
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Lismore and the Northern Rivers. Honest advice on flood height, container siting and storage through a rebuild.
locations.line: There is no writing about Lismore without writing about water, and no point writing about water unless we are going to be straight. A container is a good store and it is not flood protection. What it gives you here is a dry, lockable box that can sit on the high part of the block, hold what matters, and be emptied in an afternoon when the river starts coming up.
locations.uses: storage while a house is raised, repaired or rebuilt, tools and materials for owner-builders on a job that has taken years, not months, gear for the trades and community groups working across the district, machinery and feed storage on the blocks out through Clunes, Bexhill and Dunoon, secure storage for small businesses working out of a yard, and dry storage up on the higher ground at Goonellabah for people whose sheds are not coming back
access: Lismore is two different delivery towns divided by about thirty metres of elevation. The flats — South Lismore, North Lismore, the CBD fringe and the ground along the Wilsons River and Leycester Creek — are alluvial silt. It is beautiful soil and it behaves like every other river silt we work on: it dries to something that feels like hardstand, and after a wet week it will let a loaded rear axle down without warning. A lot of those blocks now have a raised house on them, which changes the job again, because the usable ground is often underneath or beside a structure on stands, with restricted headroom and services running where they did not run before. The hill suburbs are the other half. Goonellabah, East Lismore, Girards Hill and the streets climbing out of the basin are steep and short on frontage, with driveways that pitch hard at the kerb and back yards you reach down a strip of concrete a Falcon was built for. Those are frequently crane jobs rather than tilt-tray jobs, and the deciding factors are what is overhead and how much street the outriggers can have. Beyond town it changes again. The roads out to Dunoon, Nimbin, Clunes and Bexhill are winding red-soil country roads with tight corners, single-lane bridges and sections that have been repaired, slipped and repaired again. Some carry width restrictions after slips. Red basalt on the ridges is excellent ground and holds a truck when everything below is bogged, which is why a hill delivery will often go ahead on a day the flats will not. Send photos and we will tell you which category your block is in before we quote a truck for it.

sections.h: Being straight about containers and floodwater
p: A shipping container keeps rain out from above. It is not sealed against water pushing at it from outside, and that is not a defect — it was never designed for it. Water that reaches the door sill gets past the seals, and once it is inside, the container holds it in as efficiently as it kept it out. The second thing matters even more here: a container that is empty or lightly loaded is a large sealed volume with very little weight in it, and it floats. Things that float move, and in this valley things that move end up against somebody's house, across a road or in the river. Anybody who tells you a container is flood protection is selling you something they should not be selling, and after 2022 nobody in this town needs that explained to them.

So the useful conversation is about what actually helps, and there are three things. Height above the flood line on your particular block, which is the only one that really counts. The ability to empty it, which is why a container you can reach with a vehicle and open quickly is worth more than one wedged behind a fence. And placement that limits the damage if the worst happens — not sited where a floating box would go straight into the house, a neighbour's place or the watercourse. Keeping contents up on pallets is good practice against damp and does nothing at all against a metre of water. We would rather tell you that now than have you find out.

sections.h: Where height comes from on a Lismore block
p: Height on a block is mostly a siting decision and it is free. Put the container on the highest usable ground rather than the flattest or the most convenient, and keep it out of the overland flow path, because a lot of the damage in this district comes from water running across properties rather than the river simply backing up. Setting it on hardwood sleepers or concrete pads lifts the floor a hundred to two hundred millimetres, and a purpose-built stand or a set of stacked and packed pads can get it further. Be clear-eyed about what that buys: it makes a real difference in a minor event and against ground damp, and it is meaningless against a major one. That is not a reason to skip it — it is a reason not to mistake it for a solution. Level it properly while you are at it, door end on the high side, so the doors keep swinging cleanly rather than binding as one corner settles.

sections.h: Storage through a rebuild that takes years
p: A lot of what we do here is storage attached to a job with no clean end date on it. A house being raised, a repair waiting on a trade, a build that has stopped and restarted twice. That is what makes hire worth looking at rather than an automatic purchase: you are not tying up capital in an asset you will be trying to move on, and when the work finally finishes you ring us and it goes away rather than becoming your problem to sell. It also means you can swap to a bigger or smaller unit if the job changes shape, which buying does not let you do without selling and buying again. Where buying wins is when the container has quietly become the shed — the permanent store on a block where the outbuilding is not being replaced, or the workshop out the back that is now part of how the place works. Either way, if it is holding household contents outdoors for years, ask for cargo-worthy: every cargo-worthy unit is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard. As-is units are cheaper and are not sold as watertight, and for contents you cannot replace that is the whole decision.

faqs.q: Will a shipping container keep my things dry if Lismore floods again?
faqs.a: Not on its own, and we will not pretend otherwise. A container keeps rain out from above, but it is not sealed against water pushing from outside — once floodwater reaches the door sill it gets past the seals, and then the container holds it in. What protects your things is height above the flood line on your block, and being able to empty the container and move contents when a warning comes. Site it on the highest usable ground, keep it reachable, and treat it as good dry storage rather than as a barrier.

faqs.q: Can a shipping container float away in a flood?
faqs.a: Yes. An empty or lightly loaded container is a large sealed volume with very little weight in it, and it will lift and move in deep enough water. That is worth planning for rather than ignoring. Do not site one where a floating box would be carried into your house, a neighbour's house or a watercourse, and understand that no tie-down we could describe here makes it reliable in a major event. Height above the flood line and being able to empty it are the two things that actually help.

faqs.q: We are having the house raised. Can a container hold the contents in the meantime?
faqs.a: That is one of the most common reasons people around here call us. It arrives finished and lockable on the day, needs no slab and no approval process for a temporary store on most blocks, and it keeps household goods dry and secure while the trades work around it. Ask for cargo-worthy, since every cargo-worthy unit is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard. Set it on pads with the door end on the high side, keep contents on pallets so air moves, and hire rather than buy if the job has no firm finish date.

faqs.q: Do you deliver out to Nimbin, Dunoon and Clunes?
faqs.a: Yes, and those runs are usually easier ground than the flats, because the ridges out that way are red basalt and hold a truck well. The roads are the variable rather than the soil — winding, tightly cornered, with single-lane bridges and sections that have slipped and been repaired more than once, and some carry width restrictions. A 20ft goes out there comfortably. A 40ft needs the approach checked first. Give us the road name and a photo from your gate looking back toward it and we will tell you what will make it.

locations.name: Mullumbimby
locations.depot: the south-east Queensland depots, down the highway and in off the Pacific at Brunswick Heads
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days into town; valley drops get scheduled around the weather
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft on most valley roads; 40ft only where the approach genuinely allows it
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Mullumbimby, Brunswick Heads and the Byron hinterland. Narrow valley roads, causeways and a damp climate allowed for.
locations.line: Mullum itself is an easy drop. The valleys behind it are not. Main Arm, Wilsons Creek, Upper Coopers Creek and the roads toward Huonbrook are narrow, steep, tightly cornered and wet for a decent part of the year, and on plenty of those addresses the honest answer is a 20ft rather than a 40ft. Ring with the road name and we will tell you before you order rather than after.
locations.uses: tools and materials for owner-builders on blocks where the house is still a drawing, feed, tack and fencing gear on the small farms up the valleys, dry storage for market stallholders and makers who need everything to disappear between weekends, workshop and studio conversions on rural blocks, gear for the accommodation and events operators through the shire between seasons, and somewhere genuinely secure on a shared block where nothing much lives indoors
access: The valley roads are the whole story out here. Main Arm Road, Wilsons Creek Road, Upper Main Arm and the routes toward Huonbrook and Wanganui are sealed for much of their length and still only a lane and a bit wide, cut into the side of the hill with a bank on one side and not a great deal on the other. The corners are blind and tight enough that a rigid truck with six metres of container hanging past the rear axle is committed once it starts. There are single-lane bridges and low concrete causeways over the creeks, and those causeways come up fast after rain in the ranges — sometimes with no rain at all where you are standing — and stay up for a day or so afterwards. This country also moves. Slips have closed and half-closed these roads before, repairs get made, and sections carry single-lane control or width restrictions long after the event that caused them. We check before we commit a truck. Then there is the canopy, which people forget because they drive under it every day in a car. Camphor laurel and regrowth rainforest hang low over these roads and over private driveways, and four metres is not much when a tilt bed is lifting. On the blocks themselves, driveways are typically cut into a slope with a bank on the high side and a drop on the low one, unsealed, and finishing somewhere with no turning circle at all — a ridge-top building pad is often literally only as wide as the house. The ground is good news: red basalt on the ridges is firm and drains hard. The creek flats are alluvial and soft after rain, and the coast at Ocean Shores and Brunswick Heads is dune sand that carries a lot less than it looks like it should.

sections.h: Roads out the back of Mullum
p: The distance from town to a block up Main Arm or Wilsons Creek is nothing. The road is everything. What we need to know before we commit a truck to one of those valleys is straightforward: which road, roughly how far up, whether there are causeways or single-lane bridges on the way, and whether there is any current width or load restriction on the route from a slip repair. You will know your own road far better than any map does, and five minutes on the phone is worth more than an hour of satellite imagery.

The size question falls out of that conversation. A 20ft on a tilt-tray gets up most of these valleys. A 40ft on a side loader is a genuinely different vehicle and on several of these roads the answer is simply no. Where you need the length, two 20ft placed end to end, or with a gap and a roof across the middle, usually gives you more usable space and a delivery that actually happens. We would rather have that conversation with you before you order than have a driver stopped at a corner he cannot get around with nowhere to turn.

sections.h: Blocks with no shed, no slab and sometimes no power
p: A lot of the work up here is on land that is being built out slowly and deliberately — owner-builders, shared and multiple-occupancy blocks, places where the house is years away and the tools have to live somewhere in the meantime. A container suits that better than almost anything else. It arrives finished, it locks properly, it does not need a slab poured and cured before it is useful, it does not need power, and it can be sold on or moved when the plan changes. On a steep block it also sits on pads where a shed slab would mean serious excavation.

Where we will not guess is the rules, because they vary and they are yours to check. How long the container is staying, whether it is visible, whether it is being modified and what the tenure of the land is all matter, and shared and multiple-occupancy arrangements often have their own internal agreements sitting on top of the council position. The general shape is consistent enough to plan around — temporary, screened and used for storage is the straightforward end; permanent, prominent and altered is where the questions start. Sort it before delivery rather than after, because moving a container twenty metres once the truck has gone is a second delivery, not an adjustment.

sections.h: Damp, mould and living under the canopy
p: This is one of the wettest pockets in the state and a steel box under a rainforest canopy has to be set up for it or it will disappoint you. Three things do almost all the work. Get it up off the ground on pads so air moves underneath and the floor is not sitting against wet soil for months at a time. Keep the roof clear of leaf litter, because wet leaves held against a roof panel are what actually starts surface corrosion, far more than the rain itself. And ventilate it — extra vents at each end, contents up on pallets rather than flat on the floor, and the doors left open for a few hours on a dry day when you get one. Do not shut anything damp in there. A wet tarp or a bag of green offcuts will hold the humidity up for months on its own and everything in the box will smell like it.

faqs.q: Can a truck get up Main Arm or Wilsons Creek Road?
faqs.a: Usually with a 20ft, and it depends how far up you are. Those roads are a lane and a bit wide, cut into the hillside with blind tight corners, and there are single-lane bridges and causeways along the way. A rigid truck with a container overhanging the rear axle is committed once it starts a corner, so we check the route rather than assuming. A 40ft on a side loader will not make several of those roads at all. Ring with the road name and roughly how far along you are and we will give you a straight answer.

faqs.q: What happens if a landslip or a causeway closes the road to my place?
faqs.a: We move the date rather than gamble on it. Causeways through these valleys come up quickly after rain in the ranges, sometimes with no rain where you are, and slip repairs leave single-lane control and width restrictions in place long afterwards. We check the route before committing a truck, and we will ring you rather than leave you waiting on a delivery that was never going to arrive. If there is a firm alternative — a neighbour's access, hardstand near the main road — tell us and we will often use it.

faqs.q: How do you keep things from going mouldy in a container in this climate?
faqs.a: Ventilation and getting it off the ground do most of it. Set it on pads so air moves underneath rather than the floor sitting on wet soil, fit extra vents at both ends, keep contents up on pallets, and open the doors for a few hours on a dry day when one comes along. The biggest single mistake is shutting something damp inside — a wet tarp or green timber will keep the humidity high for months and everything in there will wear it. Keep leaf litter off the roof too; that is where surface rust starts.

faqs.q: Is a container a sensible store on a block with nothing built on it yet?
faqs.a: It is one of the best things going for that situation. It lands finished and lockable in a single visit, needs no slab, no power and no connection to anything, sits on pads on ground where a shed would need excavation, and can be moved or sold when the plan changes. Check the rules for your land first, because tenure, how long it is staying and whether it is visible all matter, and shared blocks often have their own agreements on top. Get that sorted before delivery rather than afterwards.

locations.name: Grafton
locations.depot: the south-east Queensland depots, run south down the Pacific Highway
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days; river-flat and back-road drops move with the weather
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; side loader or crane truck for 40ft where there is room to set up
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Grafton and the Clarence Valley. Both sides of the river, flood-prone flats, timber and cattle country access covered.
locations.line: Grafton is a river town and the river organises everything, a container delivery included. Which side of it you are on decides the run in. How high your block sits above it decides where the container should go. And the amount of notice the Clarence gives when it rises decides what you do about it. All three are worth five minutes before we book a truck.
locations.uses: wire, posts and strainers on the cattle country through the Orara and up the Summerland Way, chains, saws and gear for the timber blocks, dry storage for cane and small crops downriver, tools and materials for the trades working the valley, machinery parts on properties where the nearest replacement is a long drive and a long wait, and lockable storage for households and businesses who would rather have their things up high than merely behind a locked door
access: The first question on a Grafton delivery is which side of the river the address is on, because it changes the run in and sometimes changes the truck. South Grafton is the working side — the industrial land, the saleyards, wide entries and hardstand, and about as straightforward a drop as we do anywhere. North across the water, the older Grafton grid is a different job. The streets are generous by nineteenth-century standards and tight by truck standards, and they are lined with mature jacarandas and camphors that hang low enough to matter to a lifted tilt bed. Those trees are part of why people live there, so we work around them rather than through them, which sometimes means a crane lift from the street instead of threading a truck down a driveway. The bridges shape the run too: the newer crossing carries the heavy traffic and the older one is narrow, so where a truck goes over is not always where a car would. Off the town grid, the river flats are alluvial silt — deep, fertile and completely reliable when dry, and capable of swallowing a rear axle after a wet week. Southgate, Cowper, Ulmarra and the farm country downriver are all that ground, reached by roads with a levee bank on one side and a drain on the other, and it is worth knowing which paddock gate is on firm approach before the truck arrives rather than after. West and south, out through Coutts Crossing, the Orara Valley and the Gwydir climb toward the range, it becomes proper rural access: long unsealed driveways, grids of unknown rating, culvert crossings that have been in the ground thirty years, cattle on the road, and turning space at the far end that has to be genuinely truck-sized rather than optimistic. Photos from the gate and from the spot itself settle nearly all of it in one phone call.

sections.h: Which side of the river you are on
p: It sounds like a small thing and it is not. South Grafton and the industrial side is easy delivery — wide gates, hardstand, room to line a truck up, and often a forklift already on site. Give us the gate address, a contact who will be there and any site induction requirements, and it happens without a second phone call. North of the river, the older streets need more thought. The blocks are deeper than they are wide, the houses sit close to a boundary, side access is narrow, and the street trees that make those streets worth living in are exactly at the height a tilt bed wants to be. On a fair proportion of those addresses a crane truck lifting over the fence is quicker, tidier and less likely to take a limb off something that has been there a hundred years.

The other reason it matters is the bridge. Where a truck can cross is not always where a car crosses, and that changes the approach and occasionally the timing. It is our problem rather than yours, but it is worth knowing that a delivery to an address five hundred metres from our last drop can be a longer run than it looks on a map, and it is one of the reasons we ask for the full address rather than just the suburb.

sections.h: The Clarence gives you notice — use it
p: The Clarence is a big catchment and it does not flash the way a small creek does. Rain in the headwaters turns into a river height here with real lead time, and the gauges upriver mean people in this valley usually get a day or more of warning rather than an hour. That is genuinely useful, and it should shape how you use a container rather than whether you buy one. A container is not a flood barrier — water that reaches the door sill gets past the seals, and an empty or lightly loaded container floats and will move in deep water. Nothing about the design changes that. What the warning time gives you is the chance to act: to get contents out, or to have already put the container somewhere it does not need rescuing.

So two practical things. Site it high — the highest usable part of the block, not the flattest, and out of the overland flow path. And site it somewhere you can reach with a vehicle and open quickly, because a container you can empty in an hour with a ute and two people is worth a great deal more here than one wedged behind a shed. Being behind a levee is not the same as being above the flood. Levees are built to a design level and rivers have exceeded design levels in this valley before. Work off your own block's height, not the town's.

sections.h: Timber, cattle and gear that lives outside
p: Most of what goes into a container out in the Clarence Valley is gear that would otherwise be sitting under a tarp behind the shed: chainsaws and chains, wire and strainers, drums, vet gear, pumps, spare parts for machinery that is twenty years old and not getting replaced. The value is not glamorous — it is that everything is in one lockable place, dry, out of the weather and not being taken apart by whoever needed a fitting last Tuesday. Every cargo-worthy unit is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard, which is what you want when the contents are steel that will rust and consumables that will not survive getting damp. Set it on hardwood sleepers or pads at the four corner castings, door end on the high side of any fall, keep the grass down around the base and the underside clear so water and air move through, and it will still be square and opening cleanly in twenty years.

faqs.q: Do you deliver on both sides of the Clarence?
faqs.a: Both sides and well beyond. South Grafton and the industrial area is some of the easiest delivery we do — hardstand, wide entries, room to manoeuvre. The older streets north of the river need more planning because of narrow side access and low street-tree canopy, and a fair few of those end up as a crane lift over the fence rather than a drive-in. Give us the full street address rather than the suburb, because the crossing a truck uses is not always the one a car uses and it changes the run.

faqs.q: Our block is behind the Grafton levee. Is that high enough for a container?
faqs.a: Work off your block's own height rather than the levee's. A levee is built to a design level, and rivers in this valley have gone over design levels before, so being behind one is not the same as being above the flood. A container will not change that either way — it is not a barrier, water reaching the door sill gets past the seals, and an empty one floats. Site it on the highest usable ground on the block, out of the overland flow path, and somewhere you can reach and empty quickly when a warning comes.

faqs.q: Can you get a container out to a property in the Orara Valley?
faqs.a: Yes, and the constraints are the standard rural ones rather than anything unusual. Long unsealed driveways that are excellent in the dry and greasy within an hour of a storm, grids with no rating plate and no known history, culvert crossings that have been in the ground for decades, and turning space at the far end that needs to be real. Tell us about the grid and the crossings at the enquiry. Where the driveway is the problem, we can set the container down on firm ground near the road for you to shift in with a tractor.

faqs.q: Do you deliver downriver to Ulmarra, Maclean and Yamba?
faqs.a: Regularly. The ground downriver is alluvial flat — superb when it is dry and soft after a wet stretch, so a booking down that way is more weather-dependent than one into town. The roads out to the farm gates often run with a levee bank on one side and a drain on the other, which leaves no margin for a truck that needs to pull over. Tell us which gate is on the firmest approach and we will use that one. At Yamba the coastal blocks bring sand and tight side access into it as well.

locations.name: Sydney
locations.depot: Sydney-basin depots — the yards around Port Botany and out through Yennora, Chullora, Erskine Park and Minto
locations.leadTime: Usually 3–5 business days, and longer where a crane, a permit and a street closure all have to line up
locations.truck: Tilt-tray where there is a straight run in; crane truck far more often than anywhere else we deliver; side loader for 40ft into a yard
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Sydney, supplied from Sydney-basin depots. Crane lifts, narrow inner streets, strata and truck curfews sorted up front.
locations.line: We will be straight about Sydney: we do not cart containers down the highway from Queensland, and you would not want to pay for it if we did. Sydney orders are filled from Sydney-basin depots. What we bring is the thing that decides whether a delivery goes well — asking hard questions about the site before a truck is booked, because Sydney punishes a bad assumption.
locations.uses: storage on the tiny inner-suburban blocks where a garage was never built, site stores on the endless knockdown-rebuild work through the middle ring, secure trade storage where warehouse space costs more per month than the stock inside it, film, production and event gear that comes out for a fortnight and then vanishes, stock overflow for online businesses run out of a garage, and yard storage on the industrial estates through the west and south-west
access: Sydney is the hardest city in Australia to place a container in and it is worth understanding why before you order. The inner suburbs came first. Newtown, Erskineville, Surry Hills, Balmain, Annandale and Paddington are terrace country — no front setback, the front door effectively on the footpath, no side access of any kind, and if there is a rear lane it is likely to be three metres of bitumen between two brick walls with a power pole in it and a dogleg halfway along. There is no version of a tilt-tray that works there. The middle ring is more forgiving on paper and less so in practice, because the streets are narrow with cars parked both sides and there is exactly one place a truck can stand, usually directly in front of your house. Then there is time. Arterial roads run clearways morning and afternoon where a truck may not stop at all, some routes carry heavy-vehicle restrictions and low rail underbridges, and strata buildings and business parks set their own delivery windows. A Sydney delivery is not just a date, it is a date and an hour, and the hour is often decided by somebody other than us. Ground splits along the geology. The harbour and northern suburbs sit on sandstone, which is superb bearing and awkward to level on because the rock is exactly where it is and not where you want it. The east and the northern beaches are sand and carry far less than they look like they should. Out west from about Blacktown through Penrith and Camden it is shale clay that swells through a wet winter and shrinks away hard through summer, and a container left sitting straight on it will follow that movement corner by corner. And everywhere, hardstand is at a premium — even industrial tenancies here often have no spare yard at all.

sections.h: Where Sydney stock comes from
p: Our yard is in Queensland and we are not going to pretend a container for a Sydney address starts there. It does not. Sydney is filled from Sydney-basin depots — the yards around Port Botany and the container facilities strung through Yennora, Chullora, Villawood, Erskine Park and Minto — because that is where the stock sits, that is where the handling is cheap, and carting a box fifteen hundred kilometres to save nothing is not a service, it is a surcharge. Practically, that means Sydney supply is good: it is one of the deepest markets in the country, and asking for a particular grade, size, door configuration or a high cube is a reasonable request rather than wishful thinking. Inspection works differently to our home ground, though, and it is fair to say so plainly — you are looking at stock at a third-party depot by arrangement rather than walking around our own yard, so ring first and we will organise it, or ask for photographs of the actual unit on request and we will send them before delivery.

sections.h: Why so many Sydney jobs end up on a crane
p: In most of the country a crane lift is the exception. In Sydney it is close to routine, and the reason is simply that the housing stock predates the truck. A terrace with no side access, a semi with a metre and a half between the wall and the fence, a harbourside block where the house is three storeys below the road and reached by stairs — none of those are tilt-tray sites and no amount of optimism makes them one. A crane truck stands on the street, lifts the container over the roofline and sets it down where it needs to go. What decides whether it works is reach and clearance: how far the container has to travel horizontally, how high it has to clear, whether there are power and comms lines across the frontage, and whether the street will give the outriggers a firm, level footprint wider than the truck itself.

The other half is permission. Standing a crane on a public street generally means a road occupancy approval from your council, and depending on the street it can mean traffic control as well. That has lead time attached to it and it is not something anyone can produce on the morning. It is not difficult — it is just a job that has to be started before the delivery is booked rather than after. Tell us at the enquiry that the site has no vehicle access and we will build the quote around a lift rather than discovering it when a truck is already in your street with nowhere to go. Photos from the footpath looking at the house, from the back yard looking toward the street, and one straight up at the overhead lines will get you a real answer in a phone call.

sections.h: Sandstone in the east, shale in the west
p: Sydney's ground changes character across the city and it changes what goes under the container. On the sandstone country through the harbour suburbs and the north, bearing is excellent and the difficulty is geometry — shelf rock sits where it sits, so the pads have to be built up on the low side rather than the high side cut away, because cutting in just creates a channel for water to run along and pond against the container. On the sand through the east and the northern beaches the opposite is true: it is easy to work and it carries very little, so each corner casting will settle unevenly into it within a season unless the load is spread properly.

Out west it is shale clay, and reactive clay is the one that catches people. It takes up water through winter and swells, gives it back through a dry summer and shrinks, and it does neither evenly across a block. A container placed straight on it will rack one corner at a time, and a racked container is a container whose doors stop closing — which is the only part of it you actually touch. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corner castings, levelled in both directions and checked on the diagonals, deals with all three ground types. Get the door end on the high side of any fall and keep the underside clear so water and air can move.

faqs.q: Do Sydney containers come from Queensland?
faqs.a: No, and they should not. Sydney orders are filled from Sydney-basin depots — the yards around Port Botany and out through Yennora, Chullora, Erskine Park and Minto — because that is where the stock is and carting a box fifteen hundred kilometres would only add cost with nothing to show for it. The upside is choice: Sydney is a deep market, so a specific grade, size or door configuration is a normal request. You can inspect at a depot by arrangement rather than at our own yard, or ask for photos of the actual unit on request before delivery.

faqs.q: There is no side access at my terrace. Can a container still go in the back yard?
faqs.a: Usually yes, with a crane truck lifting from the street over the house. It is close to routine work in the inner suburbs because the housing stock predates the truck. What decides it is reach and clearance — how far the container has to travel horizontally, how high it must clear, whether there are power and comms lines across the frontage, and whether the street gives the outriggers a firm footprint wider than the truck. Photos from the footpath, from the back yard looking toward the street, and one straight up at the lines will get you an answer quickly.

faqs.q: Do I need council approval to have a container craned in from the street?
faqs.a: In most cases yes — standing a crane on a public road generally requires a road occupancy approval from the council, and on busier streets traffic control as well. Rules differ between councils and we are not going to guess at yours, so start that enquiry early because it carries lead time and cannot be arranged on the morning. Tell us at the quote that the site needs a lift and we will scope it that way from the outset rather than sending a truck that has nowhere to go.

faqs.q: Is there a limited window for delivering a container in Sydney?
faqs.a: Often, yes, and it catches people out. Arterial roads run clearways morning and afternoon where a truck may not stop at all, some routes carry heavy-vehicle restrictions and low rail underbridges, and strata buildings and business parks set their own loading windows and dock heights. A Sydney delivery is a date and an hour rather than just a date. If your building or complex has a nominated window, get it in writing first and we will book the run to land inside it.

locations.name: Melbourne
locations.depot: Melbourne depots — around the port and out through Altona, Laverton and Truganina in the west, Dandenong South in the south-east
locations.leadTime: Usually 3–5 business days; inner-city and laneway jobs need longer to set up
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for laneways and rear-lane access; side loader for 40ft into a yard
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Melbourne, supplied from local depots. Laneway access, tram wires, winter condensation and conversion work covered.
locations.line: Melbourne runs on local stock — nobody sensible carts a container from Queensland to Footscray — and the market asks different questions to the ones we get up north. More conversions, more fit-out work, more people buying a box for what it will become. The climate problem is inverted too: up there it is heat and humidity, here it is cold, wet and condensation.
locations.uses: cafe, bar and food-truck fit-outs built out of a box instead of a tenancy, workshop, studio and rehearsal conversions across the inner north, site stores on the renovation work through Brunswick, Northcote and Yarraville, storage for market, event and production gear between runs, trade and stock storage on the industrial estates at Truganina, Derrimut and Dandenong South, and machinery and feed storage on the small farms out past Werribee and Pakenham
access: Melbourne's inner suburbs have a delivery feature no other Australian city has at the same scale: bluestone rear laneways. When one is wide enough it is a gift, because it puts the truck at the back fence instead of on a busy street. When it is not, it is a trap — a typical lane is three metres between brick walls, with a dogleg, a power pole and somebody's wheelie bins in it, and a rigid truck with six metres of container overhanging the rear axle cannot negotiate that. The other Melbourne feature is overhead. Tram wires run along and across a very large share of inner-suburban streets, and a lifted tilt bed or a crane boom going up under a tram wire is not a risk anyone takes — which quietly rules out a lot of frontages through Fitzroy, Brunswick, Carlton, Richmond and along every tram route in the middle ring. Add clearways on the arterials, loading zones with time limits, and a CBD grid where a truck cannot simply stop and think, and inner Melbourne deliveries are as much about timing as geometry. Ground varies more than people expect. West and north through Werribee, Melton, Sunbury and Craigieburn is basalt plains country with heavy cracking clay that opens up through a dry summer and swells back through winter, and a container sitting straight on it will rack a corner at a time. Bayside and down the peninsula it is sand, which carries poorly. Along the Yarra and Maribyrnong flats it is silt. And a great many inner-suburban back yards are fill over old market garden or worse, which is fine to sit on and unwise to assume anything about. Then there is winter: months where a back yard simply does not dry out, and a loaded truck on soft lawn in July is how you get a lawn full of ruts.

sections.h: Bluestone lanes and tram wires
p: The rear lane is the first thing we ask about on an inner-north or inner-east job, because if it works the whole delivery gets easier. Measure it rather than eyeballing it — the width at the narrowest point, not the widest, and note any dogleg, power pole, bin store or low garage awning along the run. Lanes that look identical on a map behave completely differently once a truck is in them, and there is no reversing out of a bluestone lane with a container on the back once you are committed.

Tram wires are the constraint people never think of until the truck arrives. A tilt bed lifts, and a crane boom lifts a great deal further, and neither goes near an overhead wire. On a frontage under tram wires the delivery has to come from somewhere else — the rear lane, a side street, or a lift positioned clear of the span. It is entirely workable, it just cannot be improvised on the day. A photo from the footpath showing the wires, one down the lane if you have one, and one of where the container is going will let us tell you which of those it is before you order.

sections.h: Why a Melbourne container sweats
p: The condensation question comes up here more than anywhere else we deliver, and it is a real thing rather than a fault. A container is uninsulated steel with a very large roof area. Through a Melbourne winter the roof panel spends most of the night below the dew point of the air trapped inside, moisture forms on the underside and runs down the corrugations, and by morning it is dripping onto whatever is directly beneath. People find water on the floor and assume the roof has failed. Usually it has not — the water started on the inside of it.

It is straightforward to manage. Do not shut anything damp in there to begin with — a wet tarp, green timber or a load of gear brought in out of the rain will hold humidity up for months on its own. Keep contents up on pallets or bearers so air moves underneath them. Fit extra vents at both ends if the unit is holding anything moisture-sensitive, and open the doors for a few hours on a dry, breezy day when Melbourne provides one. For a long-term store, or for anything that is going to be occupied or fitted out, insulating the roof and walls stops the problem at the source rather than managing the symptom, and it is money well spent here in a way it is not further north.

sections.h: Buying a box that is going to be cut up
p: A large share of Melbourne enquiries are not really about storage. They are about a container that will have a window cut in it, a bar built into it, a roller door fitted or a wall opened up — food and drink fit-outs, studios, workshops, pop-ups and display spaces. The buying decision is genuinely different for that. If the box is going to be seen by customers, or clad, lined and painted, start with the straightest, cleanest unit you can get rather than the cheapest, because every dent and every patch of surface rust becomes somebody's labour later and labour costs more than the difference in the container did. Cargo-worthy units are checked wind and watertight before they leave the yard, which is the sensible floor for a conversion; as-is units are cheaper, are not sold as watertight, and are the wrong starting point for anything with a fit-out going into it. It is also worth knowing that once you start cutting into the side walls you are cutting into what makes the box rigid, and structural work of that kind needs someone who does it properly. Tell us at the enquiry what the container is becoming and we will steer you to the right starting unit.

faqs.q: Where does a Melbourne container actually come from?
faqs.a: Local depots — around the port and out through Altona, Laverton and Truganina in the west, and Dandenong South in the south-east. Nothing is carted down from Queensland for a Melbourne address, because it would add cost and achieve nothing. That local supply is why choice is good here: a particular grade, size, door configuration or a high cube is a normal request rather than a long shot. You can inspect at a depot by arrangement, or ask for photos of the actual unit on request and we will send them before delivery.

faqs.q: Can you deliver down a bluestone laneway in Fitzroy or Collingwood?
faqs.a: Sometimes, and it depends entirely on the lane. Measure the narrowest point rather than the widest, and note any dogleg, power pole, bin store or low awning along it, because a rigid truck with a container overhanging the rear axle cannot reverse back out once it is committed. Where the lane will not take a truck, a crane lift from the street usually will — provided there are no tram wires over the frontage. Send a photo down the lane and one from the street and we will tell you which it is.

faqs.q: Do containers get damp inside over a Melbourne winter?
faqs.a: They can, and it is condensation rather than a leak nearly every time. The steel roof sits below the dew point of the air inside for most of a winter night, moisture forms on the underside and drips. Do not store anything damp in there, keep contents up on pallets so air moves, fit extra vents at both ends, and open the doors for a few hours on a dry day. For a long-term store or anything being fitted out, insulating the roof and walls solves it properly rather than managing it.

faqs.q: Which grade should I buy if the container is being converted?
faqs.a: Start with the straightest, cleanest unit you can get rather than the cheapest. Every dent and rust patch becomes labour once someone is cladding, lining or painting it, and labour will cost you more than the difference in the container. Cargo-worthy is the sensible floor — those units are checked wind and watertight before they leave the yard. As-is units are cheaper, are not sold as watertight and are the wrong starting point for a fit-out. Also bear in mind that cutting into the side walls affects what makes the box rigid, so structural work needs someone who does it properly.

locations.name: Bendigo
locations.depot: Melbourne depots, run up the Calder
locations.leadTime: Usually 3–6 business days depending on how the run out from Melbourne falls
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; side loader or crane truck for 40ft where the yard has room
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Bendigo and central Victoria. Goldfields ground, farm access, summer fire risk and the Calder run explained honestly.
locations.line: A container for Bendigo comes up the Calder from Melbourne, which is good road, so the interesting part is at your end rather than on the highway. Goldfields ground is not like farm ground anywhere else — ironstone, quartz reef and a century and a half of old workings, and it is worth knowing what is under a spot before a container sits on it.
locations.uses: workshop gear and machinery on the small farms and hobby blocks through Strathfieldsaye, Axedale and Marong, hay and feed for the sheep and cropping country north of town, trade and materials storage across the Bendigo industrial estates, stock overflow for businesses that outgrew the shed two years ago, gear for clubs, markets and events that comes out a few weekends a year, and secure storage for prospecting and earthmoving gear that should not be left in the open
access: The run up the Calder from Melbourne through Gisborne, Kyneton and Harcourt is good road and rarely the constraint. What shapes a central Victorian delivery is the ground and the block. Goldfields soil is thin over hard material — ironstone gravel, quartz and reef rock, often at a couple of hundred millimetres — which is excellent bearing and completely unhelpful if the plan involved digging pads in. You build up on this country rather than cutting down into it. North of town toward the Loddon plains it swings the other way and becomes heavy grey clay that cracks wide open through a dry summer and turns greasy through winter, and a container placed straight onto it will follow that movement one corner at a time. The town blocks bring their own pattern. A lot of central Bendigo, Eaglehawk, Golden Square and Long Gully is older miner's-cottage stock — narrow frontages, houses set close to a boundary, driveways sized for a car of the 1960s, and mature ironbarks and peppercorns with limbs hanging exactly where a lifted bed wants to be. A good number of those are crane jobs rather than drive-ins. Out on the farms and hobby blocks it is standard rural access: long gravel driveways, gates measured optimistically, grids nobody has a rating for, and turning space at the far end that has to be real rather than hoped for. Then there is the calendar. Through the declared fire danger period a hot, dry, windy day is not a day for a truck to be sitting in dry grass on a paddock, and on a total fire ban day some work simply does not happen. We plan around it rather than pretending it is not there.

sections.h: The Calder run, and the towns off the back of it
p: Bendigo is the hub for a very wide piece of country, and that works in your favour if you are not actually in Bendigo. A truck coming up the Calder for a Bendigo drop can usually take in Castlemaine, Maldon, Harcourt, Heathcote, Elmore, Rochester or Marong on the same run, which is why we ask where else in the district the container might be going and whether your dates have any give in them. A few days of flexibility often gets a better spot in a run and a container on the ground sooner than a rigid date would. If you and a neighbour both need a unit, or you need two, say so — one movement beats two.

sections.h: Ironstone, quartz and old workings
p: This is the part of a Bendigo delivery that is genuinely different to anywhere else. Goldfields ground gives you superb bearing and almost no ability to dig. Ironstone gravel and reef rock sit close to the surface across much of the district, so the way to level a container here is to build the low side up with hardwood sleepers or concrete pads rather than to cut the high side down. Cutting in on this country is hard work with a shovel and it creates a shelf that water runs along and ponds against the container, which is the opposite of what you want under a long-term store.

The other thing is history. Parts of this district have been undermined since the 1850s — shafts, stopes, drives and mullock heaps, some mapped and some not. We are not in a position to assess anything of that kind and would not pretend to be, but it is a fair reason to think about where you put a couple of tonne of concentrated point load. If your block is in an old workings area and you know of a shaft, a subsidence or ground that has moved, tell us at the quote and we will place the container on the most solid part of the site rather than the most convenient one. Mullock heaps in particular look like firm made ground and are loose rubble held together by nothing much.

sections.h: Through a central Victorian summer
p: Summer here is hot, dry and long, and it has two effects worth planning for. The first is the inside of the box. An uninsulated steel container in forty-degree heat gets brutally hot, and anything sensitive to that — batteries, chemicals, aerosols, adhesives, electronics, anything with a rubber seal in it — is better off somewhere else or in a unit that has been vented and insulated properly. Whirlybirds or extra louvre vents at both ends make a real difference for very little money, and putting the container where it gets afternoon shade makes more difference again.

The second is what is around it. Through the declared fire danger period, dry grass against a steel box in a paddock is a problem worth removing rather than tolerating. Keep the grass cut back well clear of it, keep the underside free of accumulated leaf litter and stacked timber, and think hard about what is stored inside — fuel, oils and anything volatile deserve more thought than a general-purpose store. Keep the doors accessible too, since a container parked in against a fence line with two metres of dry grass in front of it is not one you can get to in a hurry. None of this is complicated, and it takes an afternoon once a year.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get a container to Bendigo?
faqs.a: Usually three to six business days, and it depends on how the run out of Melbourne falls rather than on the road, which is good all the way up the Calder. Bendigo is a hub for a big district, so trucks heading that way often take in several drops, and a few days of flexibility on your date generally gets you a better place in the run. If you have a fixed date — a build start, a settlement, a lease ending — tell us at the enquiry and we will schedule around it.

faqs.q: Is old mining ground a problem to put a container on?
faqs.a: It is worth thinking about rather than worrying about. Parts of the district have been undermined since the 1850s, and mullock heaps in particular look like solid made ground while being loose rubble. We cannot assess any of that and will not pretend otherwise. What we will do is place the container on the most solid part of the site rather than the most convenient one, so if you know of a shaft, a subsidence or ground that has shifted, tell us at the quote. On sound goldfields ground the bearing is excellent — better than most farm country.

faqs.q: Does a container get too hot inside in a central Victorian summer?
faqs.a: It gets very hot. Uninsulated steel in forty-degree heat is not the place for batteries, chemicals, aerosols, adhesives, electronics or anything with a rubber seal that matters. For general storage it is fine. To improve it, fit whirlybirds or louvre vents at both ends so hot air can escape, and site it where it gets afternoon shade if the block allows. If the container is being used as a workshop or anything you have to stand in, insulate it — it changes the space completely and it is worth the outlay here.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to a farm north of Bendigo out toward Elmore and Rochester?
faqs.a: Yes, and that country is generally good access apart from the ground itself. North of town the soil turns to heavy grey clay that cracks open in summer and goes greasy through winter, so a wet stretch will move a booking rather than cancel it. The usual rural questions apply: gate width at the narrowest point, whether the grid has any known rating, culvert crossings on the driveway, and enough room at the far end for the truck to line up straight. Send a photo from the gate and one of the spot and we will plan it properly.
